summary: We developed Yaku Qarpana, an accessible decision-support tool for agricultural irrigation in Cochabamba. The system integrates climatic and satellite data (including NASA SMAP, GPM IMERG, NASA POWER, and Open-Meteo), municipal cartography, and local sensors connected to an ESP32 microcontroller to calculate water balances and plot-specific risk rules.   The project addresses the daily uncertainty farmers face regarding when and how much to water by transforming scattered, complex data into clear, actionable recommendations via a web interface. Additionally, it sends direct irrigation commands to the hardware and enhances coordination among individual producers, irrigation associations, and municipal authorities (GAMC).   This solution is vital because agriculture accounts for roughly 70% of global freshwater withdrawals, and rural families in Bolivia need greater climate resilience. Yaku Qarpana optimizes water consumption and pumping energy, protecting crop yields from both water stress and waterlogging while safeguarding the livelihoods of rural farming communities.
details:
Project Details: Yaku Qarpana

1. What does it do and how does it work?

Yaku Qarpana is an automated IoT irrigation system and Decision Support System (DSS) designed to optimize agricultural water management. It operates as an integrated data-to-decision pipeline:

  • Information Gathering: It aggregates real-time data from local ESP32-connected sensors, climate and satellite APIs (such as NASA SMAP, GPM IMERG, NASA POWER, and Open-Meteo), and municipal cartography.
  • Evaluation: The system computes daily water balances and evaluates plot-specific risk rules.
  • Response & Action: It generates clear, web-based recommendations (e.g., advising whether to irrigate or wait to avoid waterlogging) and communicates control commands directly to the ESP32 hardware to automate or guide watering.

2. What benefits does it offer?

  • For Producers: Provides precise, timely guidance on when and how much to water, preventing both crop water stress (under-irrigation) and soil waterlogging (over-irrigation).
  • For Irrigation Associations: Improves water distribution coordination across multiple plots, helping prioritize canal maintenance and parcel inspections.
  • For Municipalities (GAMC): Offers territorial tracking data to support institutional coordination and resource planning.
  • Resource Conservation: Optimizes water usage and pumping energy, directly protecting the livelihoods and climate resilience of rural families.

3. What is the expected impact of the project?

The expected impact is a more sustainable and resilient agricultural sector in Cochabamba. By bridging the gap between complex meteorological data and practical on-the-farm actions, the project aims to reduce unnecessary water waste, improve crop yields, and strengthen community-level water governance among local irrigators starting from a gradual pilot phase.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Backend & Architecture: Spring Boot, REST APIs.
  • Frontend & UI: Bootstrap, responsive web and mobile layouts (with preliminary multilingual support for Spanish, English, and Quechua).
  • Hardware & IoT: ESP32 microcontrollers and local soil/environmental sensors.
  • Data Sources: NASA SMAP, GPM IMERG, NASA POWER, Open-Meteo, and municipal spatial layers.

5. In what way is your project creative/innovative?

Yaku Qarpana is creative because it bridges macro-level aerospace technology (NASA satellite data) with micro-level agricultural realities (local ESP32 sensors and rural irrigation associations) in an accessible way. Instead of relying solely on expensive, proprietary commercial systems, it democratizes advanced hydrological forecasting into an affordable, localized, and easy-to-understand web platform tailored specifically to the regional context of Cochabamba.

6. What factors did your team take into account?

  • Gradual Implementation: Designing the rollout to start with a single pilot plot alongside an irrigation association to verify data accuracy and device reliability before scaling.
  • Local Adaptation: Tailoring the software and hardware configuration to fit specific regional crops, existing irrigation infrastructure, and local connectivity constraints.
  • Usability & Accessibility: Ensuring that the interface translates complex meteorological data into simple, actionable alerts that producers can easily understand and act upon on their devices.
